<div class="intro-chapter"><p class="intro">Imagine we want to compare the bird communities of two regenerating forest patches. We could establish observation points, spend ten minutes at each and record every bird we see or hear. But if one patch produces fewer records, would that mean it contains fewer birds or fewer species? If we were surveying trees, we could establish plots and measure the individuals rooted within their boundaries. A bird may use a patch regularly without being near us during a ten-minute count, and even a nearby bird may remain silent or concealed. Its movement and behaviour influence both the ecological patterns we want to investigate and the observations available to us. How, then, can we use the animals we encounter to learn about those we miss?</p><p>We will develop this question through the same sequence used in earlier chapters: understand the ecological system, define the quantity we want to learn about, examine what a measurement actually records, then organise sampling across the relevant places and times. Animal field methods deserve extended treatment because they vary greatly across organisms and questions, but their shared methodological challenges are movement, availability, imperfect detection and the difference between an observed record and an ecological estimate. The main narrative follows a small number of worked study problems. Optional technical boxes work through estimation logic slowly, beginning with the ecological problem before introducing notation. The <a href="#ch8-explorer">Animal Field Methods Explorer</a> provides broader, expandable method guides with field-design illustrations and links to published applications without interrupting the main narrative.</p></div>
:::

## 8.1 · Animal ecology determines how we can observe a population {#ch8-s81}

::: {.env2301-update}
<section><p>Our first decisions in the bird study are already ecological. Many species are active and vocal around dawn, so an early-morning survey will probably produce more records than an otherwise comparable survey at midday. Some birds are usually detected through calls, while others are more readily seen moving through vegetation. We need to know enough about the community to establish sensible observation times and locations before deciding whether point counts, line transects or acoustic recorders are most appropriate. Even within one bird assemblage, canopy position, vocal activity, territorial behaviour and movement differ among species. One observation method can therefore provide good coverage of some species and systematically underrepresent others, with consequences for any comparison of the communities we reconstruct from the records. Now suppose we shift our question to nocturnal terrestrial mammals in the same forest patches. A daytime point count cannot simply be adapted by recording mammals instead of birds: the animals may be largely unavailable to an observer at that time. Camera traps are a plausible alternative because they operate in the absence of a person and can record animals travelling through a sensor zone at night. But camera trapping introduces a different relationship between the animals and our records. A mammal may live in the surrounding forest and never walk directly in front of our camera; another may pass it repeatedly while travelling between feeding areas. The number of records is therefore influenced by movement and local routes as well as by how many animals are present. A method chosen because it matches the organism's activity pattern also needs to be evaluated in relation to the particular ecological quantity we want to estimate.</p>
<p>Movement affects the spatial meaning of observations even with species that we can see readily. A territorial bird may remain within a relatively restricted area during the breeding season, while a wide-ranging frugivore could be recorded at several survey locations in one day. Detecting it at three points establishes use of three observation areas, but does not automatically establish three individuals. Availability also varies across longer periods. For an amphibian that calls mainly during wet conditions, differences in rainfall between survey days can produce very different records from the same pond. If one forest is always visited after rain and the other during dry weather, what appears to be a community difference may partly be a sampling-condition difference. When we develop the design, activity patterns, life stages, movements and likely sources of disturbance belong alongside the usual considerations about study area and effort. A final choice concerns which component of the population or community we intend our method to represent. Pitfall trapping with drift fences can be useful for ground-active amphibians that move across the forest floor, but it is unlikely to sample arboreal species adequately. If we want an inventory of the wider amphibian assemblage, complementary visual or acoustic searches may be needed; if we specifically want to investigate ground-active species, a correctly designed pitfall survey can be entirely appropriate. A method is not weak because it samples a particular component. The weakness arises when the conclusion silently broadens from that component to a larger community the method did not represent. The Explorer provides analogous ecological considerations for birds, mammals, reptiles, odonates, other invertebrates and aquatic groups.</p></section>
:::

## 8.2 · From animals using a site to animals in our dataset {#ch8-s82}

::: {.env2301-update}
<section><p>Suppose our forest patches contain the same number of individuals of one insect-eating bird species. We conduct one ten-minute point count in each and record six birds in the first patch and three in the second. The difference is genuine as a difference in observations, but we do not yet know whether the underlying populations differ. Some birds using each patch may not be close enough to the point during the count to be observable, and others may be nearby but silent or hidden. Calls or movements that become available may still be missed because of vegetation, background noise or differences in identification. It helps to distinguish the ecological state, the <em>availability</em> of animals or cues to our chosen method, and the final <em>detection and recording</em> process (McCallum, 2005). Each link creates a possibility that a present animal will be absent from our dataset. In practice we may combine these links into an overall detection probability, but distinguishing them explains why the same population can yield different records under different field conditions.</p>
<figure><svg aria-label="Flow from animals using the study area through availability and detection to field records" height="160" role="img" viewbox="0 0 680 160" width="680"><defs><marker id="arrow8" markerheight="8" markerwidth="8" orient="auto" refx="7" refy="4"><path d="M0,0L8,4L0,8Z" fill="#487686"></path></marker></defs><g fill="#214557" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="13"><rect fill="#e5f0f1" height="70" rx="3" stroke="#8baab2" width="133" x="8" y="55"></rect><text text-anchor="middle" x="74" y="83">Animals using</text><text text-anchor="middle" x="74" y="101">the study area</text><rect fill="#e5f0f1" height="70" rx="3" stroke="#8baab2" width="133" x="185" y="55"></rect><text text-anchor="middle" x="251" y="83">Available</text><text text-anchor="middle" x="251" y="101">to the method</text><rect fill="#e5f0f1" height="70" rx="3" stroke="#8baab2" width="133" x="362" y="55"></rect><text text-anchor="middle" x="428" y="83">Detected and</text><text text-anchor="middle" x="428" y="101">identified</text><rect fill="#e5f0f1" height="70" rx="3" stroke="#8baab2" width="133" x="539" y="55"></rect><text text-anchor="middle" x="605" y="83">Recorded</text><text text-anchor="middle" x="605" y="101">observations</text></g><g marker-end="url(#arrow8)" stroke="#487686" stroke-width="1.8"><path d="M142 90H178"></path><path d="M319 90H355"></path><path d="M496 90H532"></path></g><g fill="#61777f" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle"><text x="162" y="24">activity,</text><text x="162" y="41">location</text><text x="339" y="24">cue / sensor</text><text x="339" y="41">probability</text><text x="516" y="24">recording and</text><text x="516" y="41">classification</text></g></svg><figcaption><span class="figure-label">Figure 8.1.</span> The number of animals present or using a site is filtered before becoming a field record. An animal can be within the ecological population yet unavailable when the survey occurs (for example, a silent bird during an acoustic count). Even an available animal or cue can be missed because of distance, foliage, weather or observer performance, and detections must still be identified correctly. These stages can change among habitats and times; fewer records need not mean fewer animals.</figcaption></figure>
<figure id="ch8-fig2"><a href="figures/ch08/fig8_2_se_asia_visual_detection.png" target="_blank" rel="noopener" title="Open the illustration at full resolution"><img src="figures/ch08/fig8_2_se_asia_visual_detection.png" alt="Two illustrated Southeast Asian lowland-rainforest scenes with the same six animals. The first reveals the animals present; the second shows an example visual survey detecting the hornbill and mousedeer while a small brown bird, green frog, bark-camouflaged gecko and birdwing butterfly remain present but harder to notice. Beneath are six numbered species portraits." loading="lazy" style="display:block;max-width:100%;height:auto"/></a><figcaption><span class="figure-label">Figure 8.2.</span> Animals present and animals recorded in one hypothetical visual survey. The same six rainforest animals occur in both panels. In the second, conspicuous animals are recorded but four others remain small, cryptic or partly concealed and go undetected. The scenario illustrates how species identity, behaviour, vegetation and observer conditions affect what a survey records; the detected/not-detected labels are one possible outcome, not numerical estimates of detection probability.</figcaption></figure>
<p>The problem becomes especially clear when the response variable is simply whether or not a species was detected. Imagine visiting twenty ponds and recording a frog species at twelve of them. We can state that the species was detected at 60% of surveyed ponds (assuming correct identification), but we cannot conclude that it is absent from the other eight: frogs may not have called or surfaced during those visits, and observers can miss available animals. Repeated visits help investigate the ambiguity. A detection history of 0–1–0 at a pond demonstrates that the species was present or used the pond during our survey period but went undetected on two of the visits. Similar histories collected across multiple ponds provide information about how frequently occupied ponds yield a detection and can support estimation of occupancy under appropriate assumptions (MacKenzie et al., 2002). Bailey, Simons and Pollock (2004) applied occupancy models to terrestrial salamanders and found that detection probability varied among species and sampling methods, illustrating why a single unadjusted species list can be difficult to compare across field conditions.</p>
<p>We must also consider whether a record can incorrectly indicate presence. A call may be assigned to the wrong bird, or a camera image may be misidentified. Many of the introductory models discussed later assume that a recorded identification is correct; when false positives are plausible, the survey needs a verification procedure or an observation model that allows for them. Increasing the number of sites does not automatically repair either false-positive errors or systematic non-detection. If one forest's vegetation makes birds harder to hear than another's, additional point counts could make our estimate of the recorded difference more precise without establishing whether the underlying bird populations differ.</p>
<p>To make inferences beyond the recorded observations, we need to connect three levels. The <em>ecological process</em> concerns where animals occur, how many there are, how they move and how these properties change in space and time. The <em>observation process</em> concerns when those animals or their cues become available to a particular method and whether they are recorded. The <em>estimation process</em> uses the records, the sampling design and a model of how observations arise to infer an ecological quantity that cannot be measured completely. A model is a proposed description of the relationship, not a correction supplied by a formula alone: we may specify how detection probability varies with distance, habitat or survey conditions and use suitable field observations to estimate the unknown parameters. Other approaches obtain information about detection from repeat visits or re-encounters of identifiable individuals. Their results depend on assumptions about animals' behaviour and movement, whether their distributions are clustered or change during the survey, and the way sampling units were selected. When those assumptions are inappropriate, an apparently precise model estimate can also be wrong. These three levels explain why animal monitoring has so many methods. Animal groups differ in their ecology and observability, and questions about occurrence, abundance, community composition or demographic change require different evidence. No single field method or statistical model is appropriate in every situation; what connects them is the task of making defensible inferences about animals from incomplete observations.</p>
<details class="technical"><summary>Technical box 8A · Why repeated visits help: an ordinary pond survey, step by step</summary>
<p>Imagine we survey a pond for a particular frog. We hear no calls. Has the species failed to use that pond, or was it simply silent or inaudible while we were there? With one visit, those two situations lead to the same record: zero. This is the reason to consider more than one visit when absence or occupancy is central to the ecological question.</p>
<p><span class="step">Start with one known occupied pond.</span> For an illustration, suppose that under our standardised night-survey protocol a frog present at that pond has probability <em>p = 0.5</em> of being detected on a visit. It therefore also has a 0.5 chance of being missed. This is an assumed value for the example, not a general detection probability for frogs.</p>
<p><span class="step">Now revisit.</span> If visits represent independent detection opportunities with the same probability and the occupancy state remains unchanged, the probability of missing a present frog on all three occasions is 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.125. We therefore have a 1 − 0.125 = <strong>0.875</strong>, or 87.5%, chance of detecting that present species at least once. More generally, with K such visits and per-visit detection probability p, the chance of one or more detections is <strong>1 − (1 − p)<sup>K</sup></strong>.</p>
<table><thead><tr><th>Visits (K)</th><th>Chance of at least one detection if the species is present (p = 0.5)</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>1</td><td>50%</td></tr><tr><td>2</td><td>75%</td></tr><tr><td>3</td><td>87.5%</td></tr><tr><td>4</td><td>93.75%</td></tr></tbody></table>
<p><span class="step">What does this not establish?</span> It does not tell us how many frogs live at the pond, and it does not prove absence if four visits all yield zero. Rainfall, calling behaviour, observer, seasonal timing and equipment can change p. Repeated visits spread across a long breeding season may also violate the assumption that occupancy remains unchanged. We have used a simple probability calculation to understand the observation problem, not to prescribe a universal number of visits. Occupancy modelling in Box 8E develops how repeated histories across <em>many sites</em> can help estimate detection probability rather than assuming it in advance. See Pellet and Schmidt (2005) for a field application of repeated amphibian call surveys.</p></details>
</section>
:::

## 8.3 · Deciding what we want to estimate {#ch8-s83}

::: {.env2301-update}
<section><p>We began by asking whether the bird communities in our two forest patches differ, but that question still leaves several possible quantities. We might want to know which species use each patch, the number of species present, the abundance of a particular species, or the density of birds per hectare. Each target needs a different connection between field records and ecological inference. A confirmed detection is evidence that a species was present or used an observation area at a particular time. An <em>observed detection proportion</em> reports how many sampling units yielded at least one record. <em>Occupancy</em> estimates the proportion or probability of defined sites occupied, often with repeated visits to account for imperfect detection; for mobile animals and small sampling units, <em>site use</em> may be a more appropriate ecological interpretation than continuous residence. <em>Abundance</em> concerns numbers of individuals, while <em>density</em> relates that number to area. An encounter or activity index instead describes observations per specified sampling effort without necessarily estimating individuals missed.</p>
<p>Suppose we operate ten cameras in each forest for thirty nights, giving 300 functioning camera-nights per forest. We separate image sequences using a consistent event rule and obtain sixty detection events in Forest A and thirty in Forest B, equivalent to twenty and ten events per 100 camera-nights. Our focal species is recorded at eight camera stations in A and six in B. The events are useful data about activity at the camera locations under those operating conditions. They do not establish that A contains twice as many mammals: individuals could move more frequently, follow trails near cameras or be detected more reliably there. Even the stations with records do not directly give us the proportion of occupied stations, since use can occur without a detection. The label we attach to the response variable has consequences for every conclusion we subsequently draw.</p>
<table><caption>Table 8.1. Illustrative camera records from two forest patches. The record summaries are not density or individual counts.</caption><thead><tr><th>Record / summary</th><th>Forest A</th><th>Forest B</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Camera stations</td><td>10</td><td>10</td></tr><tr><td>Functioning survey effort</td><td>300 camera-nights</td><td>300 camera-nights</td></tr><tr><td>Detection events after the stated separation rule</td><td>60</td><td>30</td></tr><tr><td>Detection events per 100 camera-nights</td><td>20</td><td>10</td></tr><tr><td>Stations with at least one detection</td><td>8</td><td>6</td></tr></tbody></table>
<p>At the community level we face a parallel distinction. If a series of point counts produces 35 bird species in one forest and 28 in the other, those are numbers of <em>species detected</em> under the chosen sampling effort. Some species present in either forest may still be missing, particularly those that are rare, quiet or active outside our survey hours. Richness and composition comparisons therefore depend on how fully the observation method has sampled the relevant assemblages. We will return to completeness in Section 8.10. At this stage, the question is how ambitious the target quantity needs to be: a straightforward measure of site use can answer a restoration question if we want to know whether a species has begun using recovering forest, whereas a management decision about population growth may demand a design that supports density or abundance estimation. The highest level of analytical complexity is not automatically the most appropriate one.</p>
</section>
:::

## 8.4 · Direct observation: seeing, hearing and counting animals {#ch8-s84}

::: {.env2301-update}
<section><p>Suppose we decide to use bird point counts to compare our forest patches. We establish observation points, spend ten minutes at each and record all species seen or heard. This is practical for many bird assemblages because vocal species can be detected even when vegetation hides them, and an observer can visit multiple locations within a limited field period. Yet we must decide where points will be placed, how far apart they should be, when they will be visited and how the observer records an animal moving during a count. Closely spaced points may record the same individual, and locations selected only along accessible trails may emphasise particular vegetation and topographic conditions. Morning activity and vocalisation also change over the season; a valid comparison benefits from survey conditions that are comparable or from information that allows their effects to be assessed. The sample of observation points must represent the patch, just as the plant plots in Chapters 5 and 6 must represent the vegetation population about which we intend to generalise.</p>
<p>Standardising count duration does not mean that every point samples an identical area. Consider a bird calling five metres from the observer. We are generally more likely to hear it than the same bird fifty metres away, especially in dense vegetation or near running water. A count of six individuals in a relatively open patch and three in a dense patch could therefore reflect differences in abundance, differences in the effective detection area, or both. If density is our target, we may measure the distance from the observer to each bird at its first detection. Distance-sampling methods use the observed distribution of distances, together with assumptions about the observation process, to estimate how detection probability changes with distance. Figure 8.3 shows a simplified line-transect example in which detections are grouped into equal-width distance bands and a detection function is fitted to that pattern. Technical Box 8B then explains how, for line transects, the fitted relationship can be translated into an equivalent surveyed area (Buckland et al., 2001; Thomas et al., 2010). A related point-transect design uses radial distance from a point, but because the area of successive rings increases with distance its geometry must be handled differently. For conventional distance sampling, we must consider whether animals directly on the line or at the point are detected with certainty, whether their initial positions can be recorded before responsive movement, and whether our placement of transects adequately represents the area of inference. These conditions are not mathematical formalities that can simply be checked after collecting data; they are consequences of the animals' behaviour and our field procedure.</p>
<figure id="ch8-fig3"><a href="figures/ch08/fig8_3_binned_detection_curve.png" target="_blank" rel="noopener" title="Open the illustration at full resolution"><img src="figures/ch08/fig8_3_binned_detection_curve.png" alt="A graph with distance from observer on the x-axis and number of detections per equal-width distance band on the y-axis. Two sets of observed points lie around two fitted curves: one declines steeply, the other more gradually." loading="lazy" style="display:block;max-width:100%;height:auto"/></a><figcaption><span class="figure-label">Figure 8.3.</span> A simplified line-transect example showing detections grouped into equal-width distance bands, together with fitted detection functions. The observed points are field records; the smooth curves are models fitted to those records to describe how detectability changes with distance. The steeper curve could reflect a quieter or less conspicuous species, denser vegetation, or other conditions that cause detectability to fall rapidly with distance; the shallower curve could reflect more open habitat or a more conspicuous species. The illustration is conceptual. In a real survey, the fitted relationship depends on the distances of detected animals and on assumptions about the observation process.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Direct surveys can serve less demanding questions too. If we want to compare visually encountered amphibians along equivalent stream sections, a standardised timed or area-based search may provide an informative measure of observed occurrence or encounter frequency without estimating every missed animal. Such a survey nevertheless needs a defined unit, effort, conditions and scope of inference. Walking a familiar trail may be convenient but can oversample its particular microhabitats; searching only at midday may poorly represent nocturnal or rain-active species. We do not have to estimate density in every study, but we do need to know which animals our field procedure made available and what ecological statement the resulting records can support.</p>
<details class="technical" id="ch8-distance-box"><summary>Technical box 8B · From animals missed to effective surveyed area: the reasoning behind distance sampling</summary>
<p>We do not need to perform numerical integration to follow the distance-sampling argument. We need to understand how a count that misses animals can still support an estimate of density, provided we have information about the observation process. Animal surveys rarely detect every individual. To estimate abundance or density, we need information about the observation process as well as the animals recorded. We therefore describe, or <em>model</em>, the probability that an animal becomes a record under particular conditions. Distance sampling assumes a suitable relationship between detection and distance, and uses the distances of observed animals to estimate that relationship. Its fitted parameters—and the resulting density estimate—depend on the chosen model and its assumptions. The three steps below move from an artificial example in which detection probability is already known to a model in which it is estimated from field data. The numerical examples are constructed to explain the logic; they are not estimates from Figure 8.3.</p>
<p><span class="step">Step 1. Suppose detection probability is 50% across the entire area.</span> Imagine a 1 km² area in which each focal animal has a 0.5 probability of being recorded once during a survey, irrespective of location. If we count 30 animals, we would estimate that approximately twice as many were present: 30 ÷ 0.5 = <strong>60 animals</strong>, or <strong>60 individuals/km²</strong>. This is a simplified expectation, not a claim that any one survey detects exactly half the individuals. We could express the same calculation in terms of area. If density is uniform, recording half of the animals distributed across 1 km² gives the same expected count as recording <em>all</em> individuals in 0.5 km². We call that smaller, hypothetical equivalent the <em>effective surveyed area</em>: 1 km² × 0.5 = <strong>0.5 km²</strong>. Dividing 30 records by 0.5 km² again gives 60 individuals/km². We still visited the full square kilometre; the effective area is a mathematical equivalence, not a physical boundary around animals we saw.</p>
<p><span class="step">Step 2. Let detection differ between a near and a far distance band.</span> Suppose instead that we walk a total transect length of 2.5 km and consider animals up to 200 m perpendicular to the line on <em>each</em> side. The nominal area is 2 × 2.5 km × 0.2 km = <strong>1 km²</strong>. Divide this into two bands: from 0 to 100 m on either side, and from 100 to 200 m on either side. Each occupies 0.5 km². We assume for this illustration that detection averages 50% in the near band but only 10% in the far band. Their expected contributions to our records are consequently equivalent to complete observation of 0.25 km² and 0.05 km², respectively:</p>
<table><thead><tr><th>Perpendicular distance from the line</th><th>Nominal area</th><th>Assumed mean detection probability</th><th>Equivalent area with complete detection</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>0–100 m, both sides</td><td>0.50 km²</td><td>0.50</td><td>0.25 km²</td></tr><tr><td>100–200 m, both sides</td><td>0.50 km²</td><td>0.10</td><td>0.05 km²</td></tr><tr><th>Total</th><th>1.00 km²</th><th>Area-weighted mean: 0.30</th><th>0.30 km²</th></tr></tbody></table>
<p>The wider but imperfectly observed 1 km² strip now provides the expected number of records that a completely observed area of <strong>0.30 km²</strong> would provide at the same density. If we count 30 different individuals, our illustrative density estimate becomes 30 ÷ 0.30 = <strong>100 individuals/km²</strong>, rather than the uncorrected 30 individuals/km². The larger correction is a consequence of the lower overall detection probability. The example assumes comparable density across the two bands and valid individual records; the band-specific probabilities have been supplied to us rather than estimated.</p>
<figure class="box-figure" id="ch8-effective-strip"><svg viewBox="0 0 660 320" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Plan view of a line transect showing the nominal area as a pale-blue strip 200 metres each side of the central transect and the narrower equivalent effective strip as dark blue 60 metres each side. The darker strip is an equivalent complete-detection area, not a physical boundary."><rect width="660" height="320" fill="white"/><text x="330" y="24" font-size="17" fill="#274b5d" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Plan view: an equivalent fully observed strip</text><rect x="150" y="52" width="360" height="195" fill="#d8ecf7" stroke="#5e93ac" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/><rect x="276" y="52" width="108" height="195" fill="#6ba4c3" fill-opacity="0.85"/><path d="M330 52 V247" stroke="#223c4b" stroke-width="3" stroke-dasharray="7 4"/><text x="330" y="43" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#274b5d">Transect (total length L = 2.5 km)</text><text x="181" y="108" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#274b5d">Nominal</text><text x="181" y="125" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#274b5d">surveyed</text><text x="181" y="142" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#274b5d">strip</text><path d="M390 141 L382 141" stroke="#113c4c" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="441" y="112" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#113c4c" font-weight="600">Equivalent</text><text x="441" y="128" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#113c4c" font-weight="600">effective</text><text x="441" y="144" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#113c4c" font-weight="600">strip</text><line x1="150" y1="260" x2="330" y2="260" stroke="#5e93ac"/><line x1="330" y1="260" x2="510" y2="260" stroke="#5e93ac"/><text x="240" y="278" font-size="13" fill="#274b5d" text-anchor="middle">w = 200 m</text><text x="420" y="278" font-size="13" fill="#274b5d" text-anchor="middle">w = 200 m</text><text x="330" y="305" font-size="13" fill="#274b5d" text-anchor="middle">Effective half-width μ = 60 m on either side</text></svg><figcaption><strong>Box 8B figure.</strong> The pale strip covers the nominal survey width of 200 m on each side of the line (total area 1 km²). The darker strip is the hypothetical area in which complete detection would yield the same expected count (60 m on each side, total area 0.30 km²). Animals outside the darker strip can still be detected. The geometry represents the equivalence of expected counts, not an actual detection boundary; lengths and widths are drawn on different scales.</figcaption></figure>
<p><span class="step">Step 3. Estimate a continuous detection relationship instead of assuming two probabilities.</span> Actual detectability rarely changes suddenly at the boundary between two arbitrary bands. For conventional line-transect distance sampling, we record the perpendicular distance x from the line to each animal at its initial position. We then fit a suitable model, written as a detection function g(x), describing how the chance of detecting an animal changes with x. The fitted function is a hypothesis about the observation process, informed by the distribution of recorded distances and constrained by assumptions such as full detection on the transect line in the conventional approach. Rather than adding the contributions of two wide bands, we add the contributions of continuously narrower bands. The integral is mathematical shorthand for that addition:</p>
<p class="eq">μ = ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>w</sup> g(x) dx</p>
<p>The result μ has units of <em>length</em> and is the <strong>effective strip half-width</strong>, not an area on the page beneath a graph. Suppose, in a separate hypothetical analysis over the same nominal distance w = 200 m, the fitted curve gives μ = <strong>60 m = 0.06 km</strong>. Across 2.5 km of transects, the effective surveyed area is therefore <strong>2 × L × μ = 2 × 2.5 × 0.06 = 0.30 km²</strong>. Thirty recorded individuals then give the same illustrative estimate as Step 2: <strong>30 ÷ 0.30 = 100 individuals/km²</strong>. An alternative way to express this result is an average detection probability over the nominal line-transect strip of μ/w = 60/200 = 0.30. A different fitted function can give another μ; the data, modelling choices and assumptions determine the correction.</p>
<p><span class="step">Where could the estimate go wrong?</span> These examples assume that the recorded animals represent different individuals, that density is sufficiently comparable across the distance bands for this illustrative correction, and that the transects represent the landscape whose density we seek. Conventional distance sampling also assumes that animals on the line are detected (g(0) = 1), distances refer to initial locations before animals respond to the observer, distances are recorded accurately and the detection model represents how observation probability actually declines. Availability, species identity, vegetation, animal movement and observer behaviour can affect these assumptions. A density estimate must include uncertainty arising from the sampled locations and fitted detection function; choosing a plausible mathematical curve cannot correct for omitted habitats or inappropriate transect placement. Point-transect sampling uses the same general detection principle but a different area calculation, because the area of successive rings around a stationary observer increases with distance. For methods and assumptions, see Buckland et al. (2001) and Thomas et al. (2010).</p>
</details>
</section>
:::

## 8.5 · Automated observation extends coverage but changes the record {#ch8-s85}

::: {.env2301-update}
<section><p>We can now return to the nocturnal mammals in our two forest patches. Camera traps help because they continue operating when an observer is absent, potentially collecting records over days and nights that a conventional visual survey would miss. A camera is usually triggered when an animal moves through a sensor zone and produces a usable photograph or video. It provides a record of the species, location and time when identification is reliable. But the equipment is not continuously surveying every animal in the surrounding patch. It observes a relatively small zone whose effective coverage depends on sensor characteristics, camera height and angle, vegetation immediately in front of the unit, temperature and the size and movement of the animal. Camera trapping moves the observation opportunity from the observer's presence to the animal's passage through the camera zone; it does not remove the dependence of records on ecology and detectability (Burton et al., 2015). Imagine placing half our cameras along frequently used trails and the remainder at locations selected independently of trail access. The trail cameras may return many more mammal photographs, not necessarily because their parts of the forest contain more individuals, but because movement is channelled past the sensors. If our question concerns trail use this is a feature of the design; if it concerns the mammal community of the entire patch, it requires careful justification or a different placement strategy. We must also decide whether successive images represent a single encounter event. A passing mammal can trigger twenty photographs in a minute, and the same animal can return later; applying a standard event-separation interval makes summaries reproducible but does not magically identify unique individuals. Actual functioning nights should be recorded because equipment can fail, batteries can run down or vegetation can repeatedly trigger the sensor. The results become more useful when camera position, operating conditions, habitat and processing decisions are documented alongside the images.</p>
<p>Autonomous acoustic recorders provide another way to extend observations through time. A recorder can collect calls of birds, frogs or other vocal animals when no observer is present, and the files can be stored and checked later. It has an effective acoustic sampling space, however, that depends on microphone quality and placement, call amplitude, vegetation and background noise. Recording for a longer period improves temporal coverage of animals that vocalise intermittently but does not necessarily detect a quiet species or a call beyond the microphone's reach. Darras et al. (2018) compared autonomous recorders with human bird point counts in a meta-analysis and showed the importance of accounting for their different effective detection ranges when evaluating sampling performance. We should therefore choose recording duration, location and equipment in relation to the vocal behaviour and population component we intend to represent, rather than assuming that many stored recordings automatically make a more complete survey.</p>
<figure id="ch8-camera-figure"><a href="figures/ch08/fig8_4_camera_trap_events.png" target="_blank" rel="noopener" title="Open Figure 8.4 at full resolution"><img src="figures/ch08/fig8_4_camera_trap_events.png" loading="lazy" style="display:block;width:100%;height:auto" alt="Three-part illustration of camera trapping in a Southeast Asian rainforest: A, a tree-mounted camera records animals within a limited sensor zone; B, four hypothetical time-stamped encounters include repeated visits by one animal; C, numbers of animals, repeated movement, trail use, and triggering probability all contribute to camera-trap event totals." /></a><figcaption><span class="figure-label">Figure 8.4.</span> <strong>How camera-trap records arise from animal movement and detection.</strong> <strong>(A)</strong> A camera mounted on a tree detects animals only when they pass through its limited sensor zone. <strong>(B)</strong> Four illustrative, time-stamped detection events: the first three show repeated visits by Individual A, whereas the fourth shows Individual B. The identities are supplied to explain the example; in an actual survey, photographs do not always permit individual identification. <strong>(C)</strong> More camera-trap events can result from more animals in the area, more frequent movements by the same animals, greater use of the route on which the camera is placed, or higher probability of triggering and recording an animal. The depicted mammals illustrate a tropical-forest setting. Event rates are records of encounters under specified sampling conditions, not direct counts of distinct individuals.</figcaption></figure>
<details class="technical"><summary>Worked camera-processing example · How 92 photographs become field evidence</summary>
<p>A camera operating for 30 functioning nights produces 92 photographs of the target mammal. Fourteen of them were triggered within seconds by a single animal walking through the sensor zone. A naïve spreadsheet that treats each image as a separate animal would badly misrepresent the ecological information. The device has created files; we must still define the observational units for the question.</p>
<p><span class="step">Step 1:</span> Preserve original timestamps, species identification confidence, operating effort, location and any camera failures. <span class="step">Step 2:</span> Apply a <em>predefined</em> rule for separating records into events (for example, a specified minimum gap between detection sequences), and document exceptions for individually recognisable animals. Suppose this produces 12 events from the 92 images. <span class="step">Step 3:</span> Decide whether the analysis requires event rate (12 events / 30 nights = 40 events per 100 camera-nights), a night-by-night detection history, or the times of records for an activity analysis.</p>
<p>These are three valid summaries of the same files, but none proves that twelve individuals live in the camera's surroundings. Repeated passes by one animal, sensor range and route use all affect the event total. If abundance or density is required, the sampling design must supply additional information and justify an estimator. Figure 8.4 illustrates how the number of animals, repeated movement, route use and the camera's detection probability can all influence event totals.</p></details>
</section>
:::

## 8.6 · Capturing animals and recognising individuals {#ch8-s86}

::: {.env2301-update}
<section><p>Camera and acoustic records may answer questions about species use and activity, but some studies require information about individual animals that cannot be obtained reliably from distant observation. Suppose we want to compare the demographic condition of small mammals in our two forest patches. With an appropriately designed live-trapping study we could capture animals, identify species, measure body size and mass, examine reproductive condition and release them according to an approved protocol. If individuals can be marked or reliably recognised, we can also determine which animals return in subsequent sampling occasions. These recaptures provide information about animals that were not observed at all: when many of the animals in a second capture occasion already carry marks, the marked fraction in the population is probably relatively high; when very few are marked, the population may be larger than the number initially caught. This is the basis of capture–mark–recapture estimation, which requires us to understand the circumstances under which marked and unmarked individuals become available for capture. Animals may differ in their movement, their attraction to bait or their response to trapping after the first capture; some may enter or leave the study area between occasions. The number captured is therefore neither an exhaustive count of the population nor necessarily proportional to abundance under different conditions. Individual identity does allow us to ask additional questions, including survival, recruitment and movement across locations, but only when the design and subsequent analysis support them. Fish tagging studies and studies based on individual coat patterns or other reliable natural marks use related reasoning, with species-specific methods and assumptions.</p>
<p>Capture also has consequences that observational methods may not. Traps must be placed and checked with animal welfare in mind, particularly where flooding, heat, predation or confinement can create substantial risk. Handling, tagging and marking may affect later movement or recapture probability, which is both an ethical and an inferential concern. Appropriate permits, expertise and approved protocols must precede field deployment. The reason to choose an intrusive method should be the information it can provide beyond less intrusive alternatives, not simply the fact that an animal in hand yields more measurements.</p>
<figure id="ch8-cmr-figure"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 205" role="img" aria-label="Mark recapture example showing first occasion four marked, then six captured including two marked"><rect width="760" height="205" fill="white"/><text x="18" y="25" font-size="18" font-weight="700" fill="#174b5a">The fraction of marked individuals in a second sample</text><rect x="15" y="43" width="332" height="132" rx="7" fill="#f6faf9" stroke="#bacfcb"/><rect x="413" y="43" width="332" height="132" rx="7" fill="#f6faf9" stroke="#bacfcb"/><text x="27" y="65" font-size="14">First occasion: mark 4, then release</text><text x="425" y="65" font-size="14">Second occasion: catch 6; 2 marked</text><g stroke="#4a5962" stroke-width="1.5"><circle cx="73" cy="115" r="13" fill="#2d809a"/><circle cx="126" cy="115" r="13" fill="#2d809a"/><circle cx="179" cy="115" r="13" fill="#2d809a"/><circle cx="232" cy="115" r="13" fill="#2d809a"/><circle cx="469" cy="110" r="13" fill="#2d809a"/><circle cx="516" cy="110" r="13" fill="#2d809a"/><circle cx="563" cy="110" r="13" fill="#dce5e5"/><circle cx="610" cy="110" r="13" fill="#dce5e5"/><circle cx="657" cy="110" r="13" fill="#dce5e5"/><circle cx="704" cy="110" r="13" fill="#dce5e5"/></g><path d="M357 114 H392 M384 106 L392 114 L384 122" fill="none" stroke="#387489" stroke-width="3" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"/><text x="28" y="159" font-size="12" fill="#36555b">blue = recognised mark</text><text x="424" y="159" font-size="12" fill="#36555b">2 of 6 = one-third of this sample marked</text></svg><figcaption><span class="figure-label">Figure 8.5.</span> <strong>Intuition behind a two-occasion capture–recapture estimate.</strong> Four individuals were initially marked and released. If two of six in the later sample are marked, marks represent roughly one-third of that sample; under the simple sampling assumptions, the four marked animals would similarly represent about one-third of the population (illustrative estimate: 4 ÷ (2/6) = 12). The larger numerical example in Box 8C uses M = 40, C = 50 and R = 10. Neither example is a real population estimate, and departures from the assumptions can bias the calculation.</figcaption></figure>
<details class="technical"><summary>Technical box 8C · Capture–mark–recapture: why the fraction marked tells us about animals we missed</summary>
<p>Suppose our traps catch some small mammals in a defined study area. We cannot see the animals that avoided capture, but we could mark the ones we caught, release them and later examine what fraction of another capture consists of already marked individuals. The intuition is that marked animals should be relatively common in a <em>small</em> population, and relatively uncommon in a <em>large</em> population, if marking and subsequent capture are sufficiently representative.</p>
<p><span class="step">First occasion:</span> We capture, identify and safely mark 40 individuals, which we then release. Call this number M. <span class="step">Second occasion:</span> We capture 50 animals (C), including 10 that carry our earlier marks (R). Thus 10/50 = 20% of the second sample is marked. If that sample represents the population reasonably, our original 40 marked animals should be about 20% of the population. Forty divided by 0.2 gives an estimated 200 animals.</p>
<p>The simplest two-occasion expression is <strong>N̂ = M × C / R</strong>. For our example, 40 × 50 / 10 = <strong>200</strong>. A small-sample adjustment, the Chapman estimator, is <strong>N̂ = ((M + 1)(C + 1)/(R + 1)) − 1</strong>, yielding about <strong>189</strong> here. Figure 8.5 draws the same fraction-of-marks reasoning with smaller numbers for visibility; the icons are schematic, not this actual field dataset.</p>
<p><span class="step">Why the result is sensitive.</span> Imagine we caught only five marked animals on the second occasion, keeping the other totals at 40 and 50. The basic estimate would rise to 400: marked animals appear rarer, suggesting a larger pool from which the second sample was drawn. Low numbers of recaptures can therefore create imprecise estimates. The arithmetic alone cannot establish its assumptions: marked individuals must retain recognisable marks, remain available through the occasions, mix suitably with unmarked animals and have appropriate recapture probabilities; the population must be sufficiently closed to births, deaths, immigration and emigration for a simple closed estimate. Animals that learn to avoid traps or are trap-happy can bias the fraction. Designs with more occasions, individual capture histories and explicit spatial information offer more elaborate analyses (Williams et al., 2002; Karanth, 1995 for individually recognisable camera records).</p></details>
</section>
:::

## 8.7 · Indirect records: evidence that persists or moves {#ch8-s87}

::: {.env2301-update}
<section><p>Some animals are rarely encountered, yet their activity leaves evidence that can be easier to sample than the animals themselves. Suppose we want to know whether a forest-dependent mammal uses a corridor linking two habitat patches. We might search systematically for tracks or dung alongside operating camera traps. A correctly identified sign provides evidence that the species used the area during a period compatible with the sign's persistence, including when no individual passed directly in front of a camera. But the sign is generated by a process separate from our observation: the animal has to produce it, it has to remain recognisable until we arrive, and we have to find and identify it. Tracks form readily in soft sediment and may be erased by the next rainfall; on a dry, hard forest floor they may barely form at all. Counting more tracks at a muddy stream margin than in adjacent forest does not therefore establish higher abundance at the stream. The substrate has changed the probability that use will leave a visible record.</p>
<p>Environmental DNA (eDNA) extends indirect sampling to genetic material organisms release through cells, waste, mucus and other material. Imagine sampling water from several freshwater streams to assess fish species occurrence. Traditional capture gear may select certain fish sizes, microhabitats or behaviours; water samples can provide complementary evidence for species that are rarely caught, subject to adequate field collection and laboratory analysis. Yet the DNA can be transported downstream, diluted and degraded, and it can be introduced through contamination. A positive water sample does not necessarily locate a living fish at that exact point at that exact moment, while a negative sample does not prove that no fish occur in the contributing stream network. We therefore need to ask how the species' biology, flow conditions and laboratory detection process connect the water sample to the ecological quantity of interest (Thomsen &amp; Willerslev, 2015). For a catchment-scale species inventory, DNA transported from upstream may still be useful evidence about the assemblage. If our aim is to locate a breeding site or estimate local abundance, the same movement of material becomes a limitation demanding a much more detailed design or complementary observations. The general problem is similar for tracks, nests, dung and feeding signs: the ecological event and the evidence it leaves can differ in their location, duration and detectability. An indirect record is valuable when we interpret it at the spatial and temporal scale that its production and persistence support.</p></section>
:::

## 8.8 · Designing a survey across space, time and sampling levels {#ch8-s88}

::: {.env2301-update}
<section><p>Suppose our regenerating forest patches form part of a restoration landscape and we want to investigate whether forest-dependent terrestrial mammals are using recovering habitat. Camera trapping is plausible for our nocturnal focal species, but choosing the equipment resolves only one part of the study. We must specify the area and period about which we want to draw conclusions, decide what constitutes a sampling unit and select locations that represent relevant variation in the habitat. Placing every camera close to convenient access paths might generate many photographs yet sample a restricted and possibly unusual part of the forest. We could instead place stations using a spatially balanced layout, or distribute them across defined habitat strata if forest structure and restoration history differ substantially within patches. Camera spacing should be considered in relation to movement: a wide-ranging mammal can visit several stations, so records from neighbouring cameras are not automatically independent individuals or independent local populations. This does not make such records useless; it determines how we should use them.</p>
<p>There is also a choice between temporal effort and spatial coverage. Ten cameras operating for 30 nights and thirty cameras operating for ten nights both provide 300 functioning camera-nights, but sample different combinations of space and time. Longer deployments at fewer stations may increase our chance of detecting a rarely encountered species at a particular location; more stations may represent variation across a heterogeneous landscape better. The answer depends on the ecological question and on how the species moves and becomes detectable. We also need to decide what counts as a repeated occasion if we intend to model occupancy. Repeated camera nights or blocks are repeated observations at an existing station, not replacements for additional sampling units across the forest. Seasonal timing, rainfall, changes in sensor visibility and equipment downtime can change detections independently of restoration. Recording these circumstances during deployment is more useful than discovering after fieldwork that they might have explained the contrast between patches.</p>
<p>Finally, the observations are hierarchical. Photographs are nested within events, events within stations, stations within forest patches, and patches within the restoration landscape. Our two original patches can support a detailed comparison of those two patches, but they are not replicated examples of restored forest in general. If a broader restoration comparison is the aim, we need more independently selected patches representing the relevant conditions, and should consider reference sites, previous differences and other plausible drivers of animal use. This is the same issue of sampling unit, replication and inference developed in <a href="04-variability-uncertainty.html#ch4-s45">Chapter 4</a> and Chapters 5–7. A well-distributed camera survey might support occurrence or activity comparisons without supporting density estimation. That is an appropriate scientific outcome if those quantities answer the question. What it cannot do is retroactively recover missing spatial coverage, individual identities or replicate patches through a complicated analysis.</p>
<details class="technical"><summary>Worked design 8D · Building a feasible restoration monitoring comparison</summary>
<p>Imagine that our management question is whether several regenerating patches are being used by forest-dependent mammals similarly to reference patches. We have access to four regenerating patches and four reference patches in a landscape, and can deploy eight cameras in each for thirty functioning nights. This gives at most 8 × 8 × 30 = <strong>1,920 camera-nights</strong>, minus actual equipment downtime. That number describes operating effort, but it does not mean we have 1,920 independent pieces of evidence about restoration.</p>
<p>We first define the <em>patch</em> as the higher-level unit of the restoration comparison and the <em>camera station</em> as a spatial observation unit nested within a patch. Place stations under the same explicit habitat-coverage rule and use comparable camera settings. Record date, habitat, orientation, vegetation immediately in front of the sensor and failures; divide operating nights into predefined repeated occasions to support detection histories for focal species. We can then calculate observed site-use summaries and standardised encounter rates, and assess whether a detection-adjusted site-use model is plausible.</p>
<p>The four regenerating and four reference patches provide the higher-level examples for comparing patch types; the 64 cameras describe variation <em>within</em> those patches. Because patch type was not experimentally randomised, an apparent contrast could also reflect soils, location, age, past disturbance or landscape context. The appropriate conclusion may be a carefully bounded comparison of site use, not proof that restoration caused a population increase. This design illustrates the trade-offs: more time per camera can improve opportunities for infrequently detected species, whereas more camera locations can improve spatial coverage if habitat variation is the main concern.</p></details>
</section>
:::

## 8.9 · Using the observation process to estimate ecological quantities {#ch8-s89}

::: {.env2301-update}
<section><p>Our camera survey has now produced detection events and histories of occasions with and without records. What we can estimate depends on which parts of the observation process our field design allows us to learn about. If our question is whether a mammal uses a station, we might turn each five-day block into a detection (1) or non-detection (0), preserving histories such as 0–1–0–1–0. Across many stations, some histories contain detections and others contain only zeros. An all-zero history has two possible explanations: the species did not use the station during the relevant period, or it did use it but went undetected on every occasion. A basic occupancy model separates an ecological component, the probability of occupancy ψ, from the conditional probability of detecting the species p when the site is occupied (MacKenzie et al., 2002). The repeated observations supply information about p, helping estimate occupancy rather than treating the observed fraction of stations with records as the complete answer. This requires a defined site, a sufficiently stable occupancy state over the survey period, suitable replication and an observation model that matches animal behaviour. For a wide-ranging mammal passing through small camera zones, interpreting ψ as local site use can be more defensible than treating it as continuous residence.</p>
<p>Abundance and density require further kinds of information. With distance sampling, the distances of detected animals help us estimate the effective area sampled and correct a count for animals missed at greater distances. With capture–mark–recapture, repeated observations of identifiable animals help us estimate the unseen fraction of a population, while spatial capture–recapture uses the locations of individual encounters to estimate density. These methods are not interchangeable: individual recognition supplies information that cannot be recovered from a list of anonymous camera events, and distance sampling requires measured distances and plausible detection assumptions collected at the appropriate stage of fieldwork. Approaches for unmarked animals are also available, including models that relate animal movement to camera encounters (Rowcliffe et al., 2008), but they require additional information and assumptions about movement and the dimensions and performance of the detection zone.</p>
<p>We may instead choose to analyse counts or encounter indices without attempting to estimate every animal missed. A standardised event rate or catch per unit effort (CPUE) can be useful for a defined ecological comparison, provided we consider whether activity, placement, gear, observer and environmental conditions differ systematically. CPUE from nets, for example, combines the number of available fish and the gear's catchability. A higher catch rate may indicate higher abundance but can also arise when fish are more active or more vulnerable to the method. Count models that explicitly incorporate detection, such as N-mixture models (Royle, 2004), require replicated count data and assumptions that allow abundance and detection to be distinguished; estimates can be sensitive to heterogeneity and model specification. Statistical machinery should therefore follow our study question and the information the design actually contains. Reporting a defensible detection or activity comparison is preferable to presenting an unreliable density estimate merely because density would sound more informative. Whatever level of estimation we choose, we should preserve the distinction between a field reading, a summary of the sampled units, an estimate of an ecological quantity for the defined study area and a claim about a wider landscape or population. Uncertainty belongs with the estimate, and its calculation must respect the sampling units and observation assumptions developed in <a href="04-variability-uncertainty.html#ch4-s42">Chapter 4</a>. A model can use additional information in the data to address a known observation problem; it cannot compensate for unrepresentative site selection, an absent comparison level or biological assumptions that are implausible for the organisms being studied.</p>

fill="#e9eef0" stroke="#a0b5b9"/><text x="539" y="177" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" fill="#43575e">0</text><text x="23" y="216" font-size="15" fill="#334e54">D · species present</text><rect x="382" y="198" width="43" height="29" rx="5" fill="#e9eef0" stroke="#a0b5b9"/><text x="403" y="217" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" fill="#43575e">0</text><rect x="450" y="198" width="43" height="29" rx="5" fill="#2d849d" stroke="#a0b5b9"/><text x="471" y="217" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" fill="white">1</text><rect x="518" y="198" width="43" height="29" rx="5" fill="#2d849d" stroke="#a0b5b9"/><text x="539" y="217" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" fill="white">1</text><text x="599" y="130" font-size="13" fill="#87583e">Both 000</text><text x="599" y="147" font-size="13" fill="#87583e">but different</text><text x="599" y="164" font-size="13" fill="#87583e">true states</text></svg><figcaption><span class="figure-label">Figure 8.6.</span> <strong>Why a non-detection is ambiguous.</strong> These four hypothetical sites were visited three times. The left column shows which sites were used. Site B was used but yielded no detections, while site C was unoccupied and yielded the same 000 history. In real surveys we usually do not know those hidden states. The mix of detection histories across many sites, with suitable model assumptions, can provide information about occupancy and detection probability.</figcaption></figure>
<details class="technical"><summary>Technical box 8E · Occupancy: why the history 000 has two possible explanations</summary>
<p>Suppose we visit each of twenty ponds on three occasions, recording 1 if we detect a focal frog and 0 otherwise. One pond yields 010: the species was missed on the first and third visits but detected on the second. We therefore know it was present at least during the second occasion, assuming the identification was correct. Another pond yields 000. It might be unoccupied, or it might be occupied but missed on all three occasions. A single record cannot distinguish these possibilities.</p>
<p><span class="step">Two different quantities.</span> Let ψ (psi) describe the probability that one of our defined sites is occupied or used during the survey period; let p denote the probability of recording the species on a visit when that site is occupied. A basic model separates the ecological state from the observation process. For a three-visit history of no detections, we have two pathways: (1) absence, probability 1 − ψ; or (2) presence with three non-detections, probability ψ × (1 − p)³. Adding them gives <strong>P(000) = (1 − ψ) + ψ(1 − p)³</strong>.</p>
<p><span class="step">Where can we learn p?</span> Histories such as 010, 110 or 101 show that detection is not guaranteed at a used site. Across many independently sampled sites with repeated visits, the relative frequencies of different histories provide information about ψ and p together. We do not know a pond's occupancy merely because we have written an equation; estimation uses the whole dataset and depends on a suitable model.</p>
<p><span class="step">What must we decide before the surveys?</span> Define site boundaries and survey occasions so the occupancy state is reasonably stable during the chosen period (closure). An animal may use a camera zone intermittently rather than reside there, which may favour a <em>site-use</em> interpretation. Detection can vary with rainfall, habitat, observer or date; advanced models may include those covariates. False-positive identification calls for a different observation model. Occupancy is also distinct from abundance: two occupied ponds can contain very different numbers of frogs. Figure 8.6 makes the ambiguity of a zero history visible. See MacKenzie et al. (2002), Bailey et al. (2004) and Pellet and Schmidt (2005).</p></details>
<details class="technical"><summary>Technical box 8F · Encounter indices, CPUE and what standardising effort actually achieves</summary>
<p>Suppose a forest yields sixty camera-trap events over 300 functioning camera-nights. Its rate is 60 / 300 × 100 = <strong>20 events per 100 camera-nights</strong>. The denominator is a measure of operating effort, not the area inhabited by twenty animals; the numerator is a set of recorded encounters, not necessarily unique individuals. Standardising effort is valuable because sixty records collected in thirty nights are not directly comparable with sixty records collected in three hundred nights. But equal effort does not make two habitats equally detectable.</p>
<p>Imagine that Forest A and Forest B contain the same number of mammals, but animals in A regularly follow a trail where our camera is installed. Animals in B disperse their movements through dense vegetation. A could produce more events without containing more individuals. Camera orientation, trigger settings, body size and changing vegetation can similarly affect the rate. For this reason an encounter index may be appropriate for comparing recorded activity at standardised detectors, but its interpretation as relative abundance requires further justification.</p>
<p>Catch per unit effort (<strong>CPUE</strong>) from aquatic nets or terrestrial traps has a related limitation. Ten fish per net-night depends on fish abundance <em>and</em> on the probability of the gear encountering and retaining fish of the relevant species and size. Changes in temperature, flow, bait, gear or animal movement may change CPUE even if abundance is stable. When monitoring through time, record conditions that influence catchability and, where necessary, design a calibration or detection model. The standardised index is not invalid; the error is claiming a biological quantity it was not designed to estimate.</p></details>
<details class="technical"><summary>Technical box 8G · Further abundance and demographic estimators: what extra data do they require?</summary>
<p>Several approaches extend the principles already developed, but they do not provide interchangeable shortcuts to 'number of animals'. Their use depends on what we recorded and the assumptions that connect those records to animals that were missed.</p>
<p><strong>Removal or depletion sampling:</strong> Imagine repeated fishing passes through a sufficiently closed stream reach. We might expect fewer fish to remain after every effective removal pass. The decline in catches can help estimate the population initially available to capture, but only if changes in capture efficiency, immigration, refuges and the capture process are accounted for. Peterson et al. (2004) shows why even multipass estimates can remain biased.</p>
<p><strong>N-mixture models:</strong> Repeated site counts can be analysed as observations of an unobserved local abundance, filtered through imperfect detection. This is attractive when animals cannot be individually identified, but abundance and detection can be difficult to distinguish from the same repeated counts; heterogeneity and distributional assumptions may strongly influence estimates. A model-generated abundance figure is not evidence that the data identified abundance reliably.</p>
<p><strong>Spatial capture–recapture:</strong> If we recognise individuals photographed or captured at multiple detectors, their encounter locations provide information about where individuals are centred and how detection falls away with distance. Coupled with a defined detector array and suitable spatial assumptions, this can support density estimation. Karanth's (1995) tiger application is a useful entry point to individually recognisable camera data.</p>
<p><strong>Open-population capture–recapture:</strong> Across longer monitoring periods, some marked animals survive and remain in the sampling population, while others die or leave and new animals enter. Repeated identification histories can support estimation of <em>apparent survival</em> and entry or recruitment. Apparent survival may combine survival and permanent emigration; interpretation therefore requires a clear definition of the biological population and observation period.</p>
<p>We include these approaches to connect methods to possible levels of inference. Their full mathematics is beyond the core chapter and should be consulted in Williams et al. (2002) or Kéry and Royle (2016) before designing a study around them.</p></details>
</section>
:::

## 8.10 · Surveying communities: richness, composition and completeness {#ch8-s810}

::: {.env2301-update}
<section><p>Our original question concerned bird diversity in two forest patches, not only one focal population. Imagine that after several point-count visits we have recorded 35 species in Forest A and 28 in Forest B. We have evidence that at least these numbers of species were present during our sampled locations and times, assuming correct identification, but we do not know that all species were detected. A species encountered often is likely to enter our records early, while an infrequent or inconspicuous species may require many visits. If Forest B has denser vegetation or a different assemblage of vocal and quiet species, the two observed lists can differ in completeness even when the same observer spends the same amount of time in both. A comparison of raw observed richness is therefore a comparison of results from a stated method and effort; interpreting it as a difference in the underlying communities requires additional consideration of detection and sampling completeness.</p>
<p>We can follow the accumulation of detected species as we add sampling units or observation occasions. A <em>species-accumulation curve</em> plots the number recorded against increasing effort. If many new species still appear as sampling continues, our survey has probably not characterised the assemblage accessible to the method very completely. If the curve begins to level off, additional standardised sampling is adding fewer previously undetected species, although it does not establish that every species has been found. Richness estimators and methods that compare samples by completeness or coverage can help when our two forests differ in numbers of individual records or detection frequencies (Gotelli &amp; Colwell, 2001; Chao &amp; Jost, 2012). We still need to understand the original sampling units and ensure that the comparison concerns ecologically comparable assemblages. Combining point counts with a different technique might reveal species absent from the first list, but a longer mixed-method list is not automatically evidence of greater ecological richness unless the methods and effort are considered in the analysis.</p>

<figcaption><span class="figure-label">Figure 8.7.</span> Species accumulation in a simulated community containing 40 species with different probabilities of being recorded. The curve rises rapidly while common species are first encountered; continued effort increasingly reveals uncommon species and adds fewer new records. The dashed line marks the complete species pool, known here only because the example is simulated. A curve approaching a plateau suggests greater sampling completeness for the defined methods and conditions, not proof that every species has been detected. When two communities differ in detectability or sampling effort, raw observed richness should not be interpreted as an unqualified difference in their full species pools.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Composition is another part of diversity that richness alone does not express. Two patches can contain the same observed number of species but very different communities. In restoration monitoring, the appearance of widespread generalists may increase richness without restoring the forest-dependent assemblage that motivated the project. We might consequently compare community composition, the occurrence of particular functional guilds or the relative use of restored and reference habitats alongside richness. If we also want to investigate an ecological function such as seed dispersal, animal occurrence may establish the possibility of that function, but a stronger test will require evidence about relevant activity—for example, visits to fruiting trees, fruit removal or seed deposition—at the spatial and temporal scale of the process.</p>
<details class="technical"><summary>Worked problem 8H · Three claims from the same community survey</summary>
<p>Point counts in Forest A yielded 35 detected bird species and those in Forest B yielded 28. The simplest defensible claim is that under our stated method and effort <strong>we detected seven more species in A</strong>. This statement describes the field evidence directly. If the species-accumulation curve in A is still climbing steeply while that in B has nearly flattened, we should not automatically infer that their complete species pools differ by seven; sampling completeness differs.</p>
<p>A stronger claim—<strong>Forest A contains seven more bird species in total</strong>—requires us to consider species missed by the method and whether the two forests were sampled comparably. A stronger claim still—<strong>restoration increased richness by seven species</strong>—introduces causal attribution. We would additionally need a study design that addresses prior differences, landscape context, other habitat drivers and change through time. None of these additional questions is answered by subtracting 28 from 35, even though the subtraction itself is correct.</p>
<p>Figure 8.7 illustrates species accumulation under unequal detection. See Gotelli and Colwell (2001) and Chao and Jost (2012) for formal approaches to richness and sample coverage.</p></details>
</section>
